Uniform title: Jñānasaṅkalinītantra Editor: Caṭṭopādhyāya, Rasika Mohana Notes: Data entered by staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski
Revision 0: October 9, 2008 Publisher: Unknown, late 19th century Publication Country: India
Published in Calcutta at the end of the 19th century. Bengali script transcribed from the edition published by Rasika Mohana Cattopadhyaya.
Calcutta, late 19th century. Bengali script. *Jñānasaṅkalinītantra*:
Seated upon the peak of Mount Kailāsa is the God of gods, the Teacher of the World.
The Great Goddess asked: "O Maheśvara, speak the knowledge."
The Goddess said: O Lord, from what does creation arise, and how does creation perish?
O Lord, how is the knowledge of Brahman free from creation and dissolution?
Īśvara said: From the unmanifest, creation arises; and into the unmanifest, it perishes.
The unmanifest is the knowledge of Brahman, which is devoid of creation and dissolution.
From the imperishable syllable Oṃ, all these fourteen branches of knowledge arise:
mantras, worship, austerity, meditation, as well as action and inaction. || 4 ||
The six Vedāṅgas, the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive Nyāya, the Dharmaśāstras, and the Purāṇas—these are the fourteen branches of knowledge (vidyās). || 5 ||
All knowledge remains merely so long as true wisdom has not arisen;
once one has realized the state of the knowledge of Brahman, all knowledge becomes firmly established.
The Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas are like common courtesans; but the knowledge of Śambhu is like a guarded woman of noble family.
All sciences reside within the body, all deities reside within the body, and all sacred fords reside within the body; they are attained through the word of the Guru.
For the knowledge of the inner self (adhyātmavidyā) brings about happiness and liberation for human beings;
through it, all religious duties, ritual actions, and recitations come to an end.
Just as fire exists within wood, fragrance within a flower, and nectar within water, so too does the Lord,
free from merit and sin, exist within the body.
The divine Iḍā is the Gaṅgā, and the Piṅgalā is the river Yamunā;
between the Iḍā and the Piṅgalā lies the Suṣumnā, which is the Sarasvatī. || 11 ||
Where the confluence of the three rivers occurs, that is called the King of Holy Places (Tīrtharāja).
One should perform an ablution there; one is liberated from all sins.
The Goddess said:
"O Maheśvara, tell me what the Khecarī Mudrā is like, and furthermore, what the Śāmbhavī Vidyā is like, as well as what the Adhyātmavidyā is like. (13)
Īśvara said: He whose mind is steady without support, and whose breath is steady without restraint;
That gaze which is steady without looking around is itself the moving *mudrā*, the *khecarī*.
Just as the mind of a child or a fool induces sleep even when deprived of dreams,
so too has he gone from the path, left without support.
That very knowledge, moving about, is Śāmbhavī. || 15 ||
The Goddess said: O God of gods, Lord of the world, speak to me, O Supreme Lord;
how is it, O God, that the philosophical systems (darśanas) come to be distinct from one another? (16)
Īśvara said:
"The devotee shall be a bearer of the triple staff (tridaṇḍin), always intent on the study of the Vedas.
Those devoted to the discourse on Prakṛti are Śāktas; the Buddhists are proponents of the doctrine of the Void."
Or those who go upwards from here, even if they are knowers of reality, the Cārvākas—who rely solely on sense objects—proclaim that "nothing exists at all. (18)
Umā asks: "O Lord, what is the nature of the Piṇḍa and the Brahmāṇḍa? O Lord, how are the five elements [formed], and what are the twenty-five qualities? (19)
Īśvara said:
Bone, flesh, nails, skin, and hair as the fifth—earth is said to possess these five qualities; it shines forth through the knowledge of Brahman. || 20 ||
Semen, blood, marrow, excrement, and urine as the fifth—these are declared to be the five qualities of water; they shine forth through the knowledge of Brahman.
Sleep, hunger, thirst, exhaustion, and laziness as the fifth—these are said to be the five qualities of *tejas*; it shines forth through the knowledge of Brahman.
Retention, movement, projection, contraction, and expansion—
these are declared to be the five qualities of the vital air (vāyu), which shines forth through the knowledge of Brahman.
Desire, anger, as well as delusion, shame, and greed as the fifth—these are said to be the five qualities of space; through the knowledge of Brahman, one shines forth.
From space arises wind; from wind, the sun is produced;
from the sun, water is produced; and from water, the earth is produced.
The earth dissolves into water; water dissolves into the sun;
the sun dissolves into the wind; and the wind dissolves into space.
From the five principles (pañcatattva) arises creation; from principle, principle dissolves.
Beyond the five principles is the supreme principle, which transcends all principles and is stainless (nirañjana).
Touching, tasting, smelling, seeing, and hearing—this is the reality of the five sense organs; the mind is the organ that accomplishes them. (28)
The entire characteristic of the cosmic egg is situated within the center of the body;
those with form perish, but that which is formless does not perish.
He whose mind is formless shall become equal to the formless;
therefore, with every effort, one should abandon that which possesses form. || 30 ||
The Goddess said:
O Ādinātha, tell me how the seven constituents (dhātus) come to be;
and how the Self (ātman), the inner self (antarātman), and the supreme self (paramātman) come to be? (31)
Īśvara said:
Semen, blood, marrow, fat, and flesh as the fifth, along with skin—these seven are established within bodies. (32)
The body is the self (ātman), and the inner self (antarātman) becomes the mind;
the supreme self (paramātman) is the void wherein the mind is dissolved. || 33 ||
The blood-element becomes the mother, the semen-element becomes the father, and the space-element becomes the vital breath; thus the fetal mass is produced. || 34 ||
The Goddess said: How is speech produced, and how is speech dissolved?
Tell me the definitive conclusion regarding speech; observe and illustrate this knowledge. (35)
Īśvara said:
From the Unmanifest (avyakta) the vital breath (prāṇa) is born; from the vital breath the mind (manas) is produced;
from the mind speech is produced; the mind is dissolved into speech. (36)
The Goddess said: In what place does the Sun dwell? In what place does the Moon dwell? In what place does the Wind dwell? In what place does the Mind dwell? (37)
The Lord said: The moon is situated at the root of the palate, and the sun is at the root of the navel;
the vital air (vāyu) dwells at the tip of the sun, and the mind dwells at the tip of the moon.
The mind resides at the tip of the sun, and life, O beloved, at the tip of the moon;
this is attained, O Great Goddess, through the word of the Guru. (39)
The Goddess said:
In what place does Śakti dwell? In what place does Śiva dwell? In what place does Kāla dwell? By what is old age produced? (40)

Īśvara said: Śakti dwells in the netherworld (pātāla), Śiva dwells in the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and Time dwells in the intermediate space; from that, old age is produced among living beings. || 41 ||
The Goddess said:
Who is it that desires food? How does one eat and drink?
And who is it that awakens in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep? (42)
Īśvara said: Prāṇa desires food, and Hutāśana (the fire) consumes it; while Vāyu remains awake throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
The Goddess said:
Who performs actions, and who is afflicted by sins?
Who commits evil deeds, and who is liberated from those evils? (44)
Śiva said:
The mind commits sins; the mind would be stained by those transgressions.
But when one becomes absorbed in that [higher] mind, one is neither by merits nor by sins.
The Goddess said:
By what means does the individual soul (jīva) become Śiva, and for what purpose?
Tell me the cause of that effect, and how, and by what, is propitiation achieved? (46)
Śiva said: Bound by delusion one becomes a living soul (jīva); freed from delusion, one is Sadāśiva.
Indeed, you are both the effect and the cause; yet, awakening is what distinguishes them.
"The mind is in one place, Śiva in another, Śakti in another, and the vital breath in yet another;
'this is a sacred ford, this is a sacred ford'—thus do people of tamasic nature wander. (48)
O fair-faced one, how can there be liberation for one who does not know the sacred ford that is the Self?
They do not say, "This is the Veda, this is the Veda"; the Veda is the eternal Brahman.
He who is devoted to the knowledge of Brahman is a true Brahmin and one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
Having churned the four Vedas and indeed all the scriptures,
the wise drink but the whey— the essence already drunk by the yogis.
All scriptures and all branches of knowledge are remnants in every mouth;
but the unmanifest knowledge of Brahman, consisting of pure consciousness, is not a remnant.
They say that what is called "asceticism" is not true austerity; celibacy is the highest austerity.
He who is one whose vital seed is drawn up is a god, and not a mere human being.
They do not call ordinary meditation "meditation"; rather, meditation is the mind that has entered into emptiness.
Through the clarity of that meditation, there is bliss and liberation—of this there is no doubt. (53)
They do not call this [ordinary] fire-oblation "homa"; rather, that which occurs in meditative absorption (samādhi) is true homa.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) is offered as an oblation into the fire of Brahman, that is called the act of homa.
Evil karma may arise, yet merit also proceeds;
therefore, with every effort, the wise man should abandon that which corresponds to such [evil] nature.
As long as one is concerned with all the various castes and lineages, true knowledge does not arise;
but having realized the state of Brahman-knowledge, one is liberated from all distinctions of caste.
The Goddess said: "O Śaṅkara, I do not understand that knowledge which has been described by you.
O Lord of Gods, tell me the certainty regarding that in which the mind is dissolved. (57)
Śaṅkara said:
That state where mind, speech, and action—the third—dissolve, like sleep without dreaming, is called the knowledge of Brahman. || 59 ||
Solitary, free from desire, tranquil, and devoid of thought;
such a state of being like that of a child—that is called the knowledge of Brahman.
I shall now proclaim half a verse as spoken by those who perceive reality:
"The abandonment of all thought, being free from anxiety, is called Yoga. (61)
Whether for the duration of a moment or half a moment, one attains meditative absorption;
the sin accumulated over a hundred lifetimes perishes at that very instant.
The Goddess said:
"To whom indeed does Śakti belong, and to whom indeed does Śiva belong?
Tell me this, O Lord, and afterwards reveal the knowledge. (63)
Īśvara said: Power dwells in the moving mind; Śiva dwells in the steady mind.
O Goddess, he who possesses a steady mind attains perfection even while remaining within the body.
The Goddess said: In what place is the threefold Śakti, as well as the six cakras, the twenty-one Brahmāṇḍas, and the seven netherworlds (pātālas)? || 65 ||
Īśvara said:
The upward power (ūrdhva-śakti) is the throat; the downward power (adhaḥ-śakti) is the anus;
the middle power (madhya-śakti) is the navel; that which transcends power (śaktyatīta) is the stainless (nirañjana).
The foundation is the secret wheel (guhyacakra), and the self-consecrated is the linga;
I have thus declared the division of the wheels. Homage, homage to that which transcends the wheels!
Above the body is the world of Brahmā, and below it is indeed Pātāla;
the physical frame is shaped like a tree, with its roots above and its branches below.
The Goddess said: O Śiva, O Śaṅkara, O Īśāna, O Supreme Lord, tell me:
O God, how are there ten vital airs and indeed ten gates? (69)
Īśvara said: The vital air Prāṇa is situated in the heart; Apāna is situated in the anus; Samāna is in the region of the navel, while Udāna rests in the throat.
Vyāna is all-pervading, residing in every limb of the body;
Nāga is the upward-moving wind, and Kūrma is established at the sacred fords (tīrthas). || 71 ||
When [the body] is agitated, Kṛkara enters; likewise, Devadatta enters during yawning; and Dhanañjaya enters during the resonance of sound and subsides when it is stilled.
This wind, which is without support, is esteemed by yogis as their yoga;
the nine gates are perceptible, and the tenth is said to be the mind. (73)
The Goddess said:
"Tell me also of the differentiation of the channels (nāḍīs) situated within all my limbs;
how the power Kuṇḍalinī has given birth to the ten channels."
Īśvara said:
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, as well as Suṣumnā which ascends upwards, Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Prasavā, and Gamanāyatā—[these are the channels]. (75)
Alambusā and Yaśā are situated on the right side, while Kula and Śaṅkhinī are established on the left side. (76)
Within these ten channels, which give rise to various other channels, seventy-two thousand channels are said to exist in the body. (77)
The yogi who discovers these is a yogi characterized by true yoga;
she is the goddess of the channel of knowledge, the bestower of perfection upon yogis. (78)
The Goddess said: O Mahādeva, Lord of Beings, O Supreme Lord, tell me:
how is it that there are three gods, O God, and how are there three states and three qualities?
Īśvara said: Brahmā abides in the state of rajas; Hari abides in the state of sattva;
Rudra abides in the state of krodha (anger); these three gods are the three guṇas.
The three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—are one single form;
for him whose mind perceives them as diverse, liberation does not arise. (81)
Brahmā exists in the form of vigor, Hari abides in the form of wind, and Rudra abides in the form of mind; these three gods are the three qualities (guṇas). || 82 ||

Brahmā abides in the state of compassion (dayā), Hari abides in the state of purity (śuddha), and Rudra abides in the state of fire (agni); these are the three gods who are the three qualities (guṇas).
The one true Being is the Supreme Brahman, the entire world of moving and non-moving things;
for him whose mind perceives manifold existence, liberation does not arise. (84)
I am the creation, I am time, I am Brahmā, and I am Hari;
I am Rudra as well, I am the void, and I am the all-pervading, stainless one.
O Goddess, I am the self of all, free from desire, and like the sky;
my own mind is pure by its very nature—I am that very one, without a doubt. (86)
One should be a conqueror of the senses, brave, a celibate student, and highly wise; one should be truthful, devoted, a donor, steadfast, and intent upon the welfare of others. || 87 ||
Celibacy has austerity as its root; compassion is recorded as the root of dharma.
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in the dharma of compassion. || 88 ||
The Goddess said: O Lord of Yoga, O Lord of the World, O Beloved of Umā’s life!
How is it that Veda, twilight rites, austerity, meditation, the performance of fire-offerings, and lineage [are all one]? (89)
Īśvara said:
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit that is identical to the knowledge of Brahman.
Whatever merit a pure person obtains at all sacred fords at all times,
that does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit equal to the knowledge of Brahman.
Neither a friend, nor sons, nor a father, nor kinsmen, nor even a master is equal to the Guru; such is that supreme state which has been perceived. 92.
There is no teacher of knowledge equal to the Guru, nor any sacred ford, nor any deities;
indeed, there is nothing whatsoever equal to the Guru, for it is by him that the supreme state is perceived.
If a teacher should impart even a single syllable to a disciple,
there is no object on earth by giving which he could become free from his debt.
The knowledge of Brahman, which is well-guarded, must not be given to just anyone; it is bestowed by the true guru only upon that devotee who possesses [true] devotion. 95.
The wise man should abandon the mantra, worship, austerity, meditation, fire-offering, recitation, the ritual of bali, renunciation, and all worldly activities. 96.
From association arise many faults; from non-attachment arise many virtues.
Therefore, with every effort, an ascetic should renounce attachment. (97)
The letter *a* is to be known as *sāttvika*, the letter *u* is remembered as *rājasa*, and the letter *m* is declared to be *tāmasa*; by these three, *prakṛti* is said to be expressed.

The syllable *akṣara* is said to be primordial nature (*prakṛti*), while *sakṣara* is the Lord himself (*īśvara*). Indeed, that primordial nature, bound by the qualities (*guṇa*), has emerged from the Lord. (99)
That Māyā is the protective power (śakti) who effects creation and dissolution;
she is ignorance, the deluder, the illustrious one whose form is sound. 100.
The letter *a* is the Ṛgveda, the letter *u* is said to be the Yajurveda, and the letter *m* is the Sāmaveda; yet it is joined with all three in the Atharvaveda. (101)
The syllable Oṃ, when protracted, should be known as having three sounds (trināda).
Furthermore, the letter A is said to be the Bhūrloka, and the letter U is called Bhuvar. (102)
The letter *ma*, together with its consonant, is ordained as the world of the gods (*svarloka*);
by means of these three syllables, the Self (*ātman*) is established. (103)
The letter *a* is to be known as the earth, endowed with a yellow color;
the letter *u*, however, is said here to be the intermediate space, having the color of lightning.
The letter *ma* should be known as the vowel, conjoined with the color white;
the single-syllabled Brahman, the eternal, is established as *oṃ*. || 105 ||
One should always be firm in posture and free from anxiety and sleep;
in this way one becomes a yogi, and not otherwise—so it was spoken by Śiva. 106.
He who recites this constantly and hears it day after day, with his soul purified of all sins, goes to the world of Śiva. || 107 ||
The Goddess said:
Tell me the characteristic of the gross; how is the mind dissolved? And tell me of the ultimate reality, of Nirvāṇa, and the characteristics of the gross and the subtle. (108)
Śiva said:
O Goddess, by that knowledge through which one is no longer possessed of sin,
[one perceives] earth, water, fire, air, and space itself.
And he exists in a gross form, as subtle, and otherwise situated.
Thus ends the Jñānasaṅkalinītantra.
